name: ChatGPT face rating

card.summary: Uploading face photos to ChatGPT or similar AI tools to get a numeric rating and a feature-by-feature breakdown that people use as a checklist for what to improve.
card.note: Outputs vary with the prompt and photo, and scores are generated text rather than measurements.

quick.overview:
ChatGPT face rating means giving an AI chatbot front and side photos and asking it to rate attractiveness and analyse features such as face shape, jawline, eye area and skin. The output is usually a score out of ten plus a breakdown and a list of suggested improvements, which some people use as a looksmaxxing to-do list.

On looksmax.org, members share prompts and results, including "rating guides" they paste in so the model scores against a chosen framework. Reactions vary: some say results are consistent, others say the scores are flattering or can be steered by the prompt. No published study has tested such ratings against human judgments.
quick.how: People upload two or three photos (front and profile, neutral lighting), paste a prompt or a rating guide, and post the result in a thread. Some then ask follow-up questions about which features to work on.
quick.risks: Photos are sent to a third-party service, so privacy settings matter. Scores are generated text and can shift with wording, angle and lighting, and forum members note that results can be flattering or contradictory. Some users report the ratings affecting how they feel about their looks.

lead: ChatGPT face rating is the practice of uploading photos of a face to ChatGPT or a similar multimodal chatbot and asking it to score attractiveness and analyse features. A typical reply gives a number out of ten, a section-by-section breakdown of face shape, symmetry, jaw, eye area and skin, and a list of suggested improvements. People use the breakdown as a checklist for what to work on, and as an on-demand second opinion that does not require posting photos for strangers to rate.[1][2]

The practice grew out of a much older habit. Looksmaxxing communities have rated faces since the 2010s, when incel and manosphere forums such as PUAHate, Sluthate and Lookism.net built the PSL scale, usually a 1 to 8 ladder of facial attractiveness.[4] Chatbots that can read images added a new route to the same kind of feedback. On looksmax.org, members share prompts, "rating guides" and pasted outputs, and argue about whether the scores mean anything.[1][2][3]

Published research on the topic is small and recent. Studies have tested general-purpose multimodal models on facial analysis tasks and on attractiveness scoring of manipulated profile images, with mixed agreement with human or clinician judgments.[8][9] No published study has yet tested chatbot attractiveness scores as a predictor of how real-world raters would score a given face.

angle.text: Users treat the AI breakdown as a checklist of features to work on, for example skin, jaw or eye area. It gives feedback on demand without posting photos for forum rating.

Score out of 10 and a feature breakdown

paras: Members typically upload two or three photos, a front view and a profile, in even lighting, then paste a prompt. Some prompts are one line asking for a rating; others are long documents that define scoring categories and tiers so the model scores against a chosen framework.[2][3] Outputs seen in forum threads often open with a photo-quality check, then break the face into structure, eye area, skin and symmetry, and end with a final number and a list of suggested enhancements.[1][2]

One looksmax.org thread presents a "rating primer" that its author says was inspired by an earlier member's thread: the user asks the model to rate according to a guide, sends the guide, and then sends two front photos. The author notes that users without a paid plan may be limited in how many images they can send in one conversation.[3] A reply in the same thread asks whether the method was tested on many people; the author answers that the ratings are consistent.[3]

A second pattern is the follow-up question. After a score, users ask which features would change it most, for example skin, jaw definition or eye-area features, and treat the answer as a to-do list for softmaxxing (non-invasive improvement such as skincare, grooming and fitness) or, less often, for procedures.[1][4]

Users often name the prompt or persona they used. One thread shares a result from a custom tool nicknamed "Aetherion", which another member had recommended as an honest rater; the output was headed "brutally objective" and scored the poster 8.7/10 with a tier label.[2] Another thread shows a long front-view analysis with sub-headings for face shape, cheekbones, jaw, chin, lower third and eye area, which another member asked to have reformatted in a different style.[1]

These examples show the main feature of the practice: the output format, scale and tone are largely set by the prompt. Users change the wording to get a harsher or gentler register, and the labels ("elite tier", "model-tier angularity") come from the framework the prompt supplies or from the model's own phrasing rather than from a measurement.[1][2]

Reactions on looksmax.org are split. Some members report that the model is consistent across attempts and share results as a quick benchmark.[3] Others dismiss the output; one reply to the 8.7/10 post says not to believe anything the model says, and a second reply points to a suggestion in the output that a user could train a forehead muscle to improve the brow ridge, which the replier regarded as implausible.[2]

A recurring theme in the threads is that the result depends on the photo and the prompt, so members compare outputs for the same face across prompts and treat the number as relative rather than absolute.[1][2][3]

Algorithmic face scoring pre-dates chatbots. In 2016 the Beauty.AI contest, run by Youth Laboratories, invited more than 60,000 people to submit photos to be judged by algorithms assessing features such as symmetry, wrinkles and apparent age. Its winners were overwhelmingly white, which drew criticism; organisers said lack of training data and poor handling of dark skin in low light may have contributed and promised to address it.[7]

Academic work on automated beauty prediction uses labelled datasets of faces rated by people. A systematic review of human facial beauty research screened 1,253 studies, assessed 44, and concluded that the datasets were not comparable and that no quantitative definition of beauty had been established.[11] One computational study found that sparsity in a neural network explained up to 28 percent of the variance in beauty scores, rising to 47 percent when combined with a feature-based measure.[12] A 2026 review in the Journal of Medical Internet Research examines bias in AI facial-aesthetic models and proposes a framework for reducing homogenising effects in training.[13]

Human research on attractiveness itself reports that averaged faces tend to be rated as more attractive, that symmetry is often rated favourably, and that agreement among raters across cultures is substantial, with some features showing more cultural variation than others.[5]

Image-capable models became part of ChatGPT through multimodal releases, with the GPT-4o model of May 2024 described as handling text, image, audio and video.[6] Because uploads go to a third-party service, users who want to limit data use look at the opt-out for chat data being used to train future models and at Memory features.[6] Forum members sometimes crop or blur background details before uploading, though the threads do not describe a standard routine.[1][2]

The models also have built-in behaviours. In the 2026 profile-image study below, both ChatGPT-4.0 and Gemini 1.5 Pro produced attractiveness scores but declined to give surgical recommendations, citing built-in restrictions.[9]
No studies have examined ChatGPT face rating as a looksmaxxing practice. Related research has tested multimodal language models on facial analysis tasks.

A 2025 study in the Journal of Clinical Medicine gave four multimodal models (ChatGPT-4o, ChatGPT-4, Gemini 1.5 Pro and Claude 3.5 Sonnet) 15 computer-generated face images and compared their answers with a plastic surgeon's assessment and manual measurements. On qualitative items such as skin texture and overall symmetry, mean accuracy ranged from 0.52 to 0.61, highest for ChatGPT-4o. On facial-ratio tasks (equal fifths, thirds, golden ratio) accuracy was lower, with Gemini 1.5 Pro highest at 0.39. Agreement was poor to high on qualitative items and generally near or below zero on quantitative ones. The authors wrote that the models are not ready to replace manual clinical assessment but may help with general feature analysis, and attributed the weak numeric results to limits in spatial reasoning and fine-detail extraction.[8]

A 2026 study in the International Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery showed digitally manipulated profile images of one female and one male model at nine jaw positions to orthodontists, maxillofacial surgeons and laypeople (72 raters in all), and asked ChatGPT-4.0 and Gemini 1.5 Pro for attractiveness scores as an exploratory comparison. Human ratings for the female model peaked at a mildly retrusive position and for the male model rose with greater projection. Agreement between humans and the AI models varied: Gemini aligned more closely for the female model and ChatGPT-4.0 for the male model. The authors described the findings as exploratory and model-specific.[9]

A 2026 survey of 288 Brazilian adults found that AI-generated post-treatment orthodontic images were rated as more attractive than real post-treatment photos (mean 68.8 versus 54.4 on a 100-point scale), and participants often could not tell which were AI-generated. This concerns image generation rather than rating, but it is part of the research on how AI-processed faces are perceived.[10]

Looksmax.org members themselves raise reliability concerns: scores that differ between prompts, flattering outputs, and implausible advice.[2][3] Press coverage of the wider looksmaxxing scene has focused on rating culture and its effects, including a March 2026 critique in The New Yorker by Becca Rothfeld, who objected to the ranking of people, and coverage of the mental-health concerns that critics link to the community.[4]
Critics of the PSL scale describe it as pseudoscientific,[4] while proponents of AI rating describe it as a private, instant alternative to public rating threads.[1][3]

Related practices include forum rate-me threads, PSL scoring, canthal tilt and facial-ratio analysis, face-shape and golden-ratio apps, and photo-based skin analysis tools. Chatbot rating is typically used alongside these rather than instead of them.[1][4]

timeline.event: Incel and manosphere forums (PUAHate, Sluthate, Lookism.net) create the PSL scale to rate faces.[4]
Beauty.AI invites 60,000+ photo submissions for algorithmic judging; its winners spark a bias controversy.[7]
A systematic review of human facial beauty research finds no agreed quantitative definition of beauty.[11]
A looksmax.org member posts a "rating primer" for having ChatGPT score photos against a guide.[3]
GPT-4o released as a model handling text, image, audio and video; members share custom-prompt ratings such as the 8.7/10 result.[2][6]
Journal of Clinical Medicine study compares four multimodal models with a surgeon on facial analysis; "Chatgpt rate me" thread posts full front-view breakdowns.[1][8]
A study of ChatGPT-4.0 and Gemini 1.5 Pro scoring manipulated profile images appears in the International Journal of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery.[9]

lore.intro: Threads on looksmax.org share AI rating prompts and results and debate their reliability; the practice sits alongside older forum rating habits.[1][2][3][4]

claims.claim: ChatGPT ratings are accurate and consistent when given a rating guide.
claims.believers: The author of a rating-method thread says results are consistent and replied to a doubter that the output is "pretty accurate and consistent".[3]
claims.experts: No published study has compared chatbot face scores with human attractiveness ratings at scale; a small exploratory study found agreement with human raters varied by model and by the sex of the face shown.[9]

claims.believers: A member shared an 8.7/10 result labelled brutally objective and said another user had called the prompt honest.[2]
claims.experts: The output format and tone follow the prompt; a 2025 study found multimodal models scored poorly to moderately on quantitative facial measures compared with a surgeon.[8]

claims.claim: The breakdown shows which features to improve.
claims.believers: Users treat the feature-by-feature sections as a checklist for skin, jaw, eye area and similar.[1][2]
claims.experts: The same study found the models more accurate on qualitative skin and symmetry observations (accuracy 0.52 to 0.61) than on ratios.[8]

claims.claim: The AI can tell you your PSL tier.
claims.believers: Members paste PSL-style guides so the model assigns tier labels such as "upper-elite".[2][3]
claims.experts: The PSL scale originated on 2010s forums and critics describe it as pseudoscientific; attractiveness research reports no agreed quantitative definition of beauty.[4][11]

claims.claim: AI rating beats posting for human ratings.
claims.believers: Users cite speed, privacy from other forum members and the ability to rerun with different prompts.[1][3]
claims.experts: Reviews of AI facial-aesthetic tools discuss bias from training data and homogenised beauty standards.[7][13]

claims.claim: Model advice on features is reliable (for example training a muscle to change the brow ridge).
claims.believers: The 8.7/10 thread included advice of this kind among the outputs.[2]
claims.experts: A replier in the thread called it implausible; the 2026 orthognathic study found the models declined to give surgical recommendations at all.[2][9]
